cards.title: Introduction to Java Architecture
cards.content:
Understanding JVM, JRE, and JDK

To master Java, you must understand how your code runs. Java is platform-independent because of its write-once, run-anywhere design philosophy.

  • JDK (Java Development Kit): The full developer software suite. Contains JRE, compilers (javac), and tools.
  • JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment in which Java applications run. Contains JVM and core library classes.
  • JVM (Java Virtual Machine): The engine that executes Java bytecode by converting it into machine code.

cards.title: Java Primitive Data Types
cards.content:
Primitive Types in Java

Java has 8 primitive data types predefined by the language:

  • Integers: byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), long (64-bit).
  • Floating-Points: float (32-bit), double (64-bit).
  • Characters: char (16-bit Unicode).
  • Logical: boolean (true/false).

Example definition:

int index = 5;
double temperature = 98.6;
boolean isValid = true;

cards.title: Control Flow Statements
cards.content:
Directing Program Execution

Java supports standard control flow mechanisms to branch and repeat processes:

Conditionals

Using if-else structures or the switch expression/statement to execute logic dynamically.

Loops

  • for loop: Best for running block code a defined number of times.
  • while loop: Runs while a boolean statement remains true.
  • do-while loop: Guarantees the block runs at least once before testing the condition.

cards.title: The Pillars of OOP
cards.content:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java

Java is built entirely around OOP principles, which focus on structuring program logic around objects rather than actions.

  • Encapsulation: Hiding internal data (using private variables) and exposing access via public getters/setters.
  • Inheritance: Allowing a new class (subclass) to adopt state and behavior from an existing class (superclass) using the extends keyword.
  • Polymorphism: The ability of a single interface or class to take on different forms (e.g., dynamic method overriding).
  • Abstraction: Hiding execution details and showing only external functional interfaces (using interfaces and abstract classes).

cards.title: Classes, Objects, and Methods
cards.content:
Defining Behavior and State

A class serves as a blueprint from which individual objects are instantiated.

public class Dog {
    // Instance Variable
    private String breed;

    // Constructor
    public Dog(String breed) {
        this.breed = breed;
    }

    // Method
    public void bark() {
        System.out.println("Woof!");
    }
}

Instantiating and using this class requires the use of the new keyword:

Dog myDog = new Dog("Beagle");
myDog.bark();

options.text: Overriding defines two methods with the same name but different argument lists inside the same class.
Overloading allows a subclass to define a method with the same name, parameters, and return type as one inherited from its superclass.
Overloading represents static polymorphism (compile-time resolved), whereas Overriding represents dynamic polymorphism (runtime resolved).
There is no functional distinction between overloading and overriding in modern Java.
